passages.original: taceant], et signorum meorum multitudinem lingua invidens non loquatur, tamen lapides ipsi, et fundamenta murorum, et parietum aedificatio meam poterunt magnitudinem personare. Quod ut significantius fiat, ponamus litteraturae quoque sae- cularis exempla. Crispus (Sallustius) loquitur in Historiis : « Saguntini fide atque aerumnis inclyti, prae mortalibus, studio majore quam 3 opibus, quippe apud quos [Al. queis] etiam tum semiruta moenia, domus intectae, parietesque templorum ambusti, manus Punicas ostentabant.
passages.english: be silent], and an envious tongue should not speak of the multitude of my signs, still the very stones, and the foundations of the walls, and the structure of the house-walls will be able to proclaim my greatness. To make this clearer, let us set out examples from secular literature as well. Crispus (Sallust) says in the Histories: "The Saguntines, renowned beyond [other] mortals for their loyalty and their hardships, with greater zeal than resources; for among them even then the half-ruined city walls, the roofless houses, and the burnt walls of the temples displayed the hands of the Carthaginians."
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; "be silent]" completes a variant reading begun in the preceding context ("[Al. taceant]", i.e. another reading has taceant for tacerent). The bracketed "[Al. queis]" records a variant reading (queis for quos) with no difference in sense and is not translated. The stray "3" before "opibus" is taken as a footnote mark and omitted. The Sallust fragment is elliptical (no main verb for the first clause); "prae mortalibus, studio majore quam opibus" is rendered literally.
